key: So mighty is his greatness; yea, greater than this is Purusa. All creatures are one-fourth of him, three-fourths eternal life in heaven.
s: Having called Purusa all that was and will be, the hymn measures him; Sāyaṇa, on 10.90.3, reads the world of all three times as his greatness, not his true nature, and the quarter as marking the world small beside Brahman, which has no measure.

evidence.gloss: The world, as much as there is of it, in the form of past, future and present: all this much is the greatness of this Purusa, his own particular power, not his real nature; his real self is greater than that greatness … though the supreme Brahman, having no measure, cannot be set out in four quarters, still a quarter is spoken of because what is meant is that this world is small compared with the nature of Brahman.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok; ref Rig Veda 10.90.3 and at [926,3] match). The plain sense recalls 10.90.2 (Purusa is all that has been and is to be) and says the hymn then measures him: faithful, and it repeats no four-word run of the key. Opened the whole Sanskrit commentary on 10.90 in the packet (verses 1 to 4 are commented as one block): on verse 3 Sāyaṇa takes the world of past, future and present as Purusa’s greatness, his power, and not his real nature (na tu tasya vāstavasvarūpam), and says that although Brahman has no measure (iyattābhāvāt) the quarter is named because this world is small beside Brahman’s nature. The reading follows these words exactly. Wilson’s translation of 10.90.3 agrees in sense. Revision 336240 dated 2022-04-20 by the Wikisource API. Gate ok.
